pos: n. (chief captain of Abimelech's host at Gerar)
etymology: Of Philistine derivation, perhaps meaning mouth of all or spokesman. He stands beside his king in two covenant-makings, one with Abraham and one with Isaac, a generation apart.
biblical_def: A pagan general opens the episode with an observation about Abraham that Abraham had not made about himself: “And it came to pass at that time, that Abimelech and Phichol the chief captain of his host spake unto Abraham, saying, God is with thee in all that thou doest” (Genesis 21:22). They had come to ask for a sworn treaty, and they got one: “Thus they made a covenant at Beersheba: then Abimelech rose up, and Phichol the chief captain of his host, and they returned into the land of the Philistines” (Genesis 21:32). A generation later the same office, and by the same name, appears before Isaac: “Then Abimelech went to him from Gerar, and Ahuzzath one of his friends, and Phichol the chief captain of his army” (Genesis 26:26). Isaac asks why they have come, seeing they hated him and sent him away, and they answer in the identical terms Phichol used to his father: “And they said, We saw certainly that the LORD was with thee: and we said, Let there be now an oath betwixt us, even betwixt us and thee, and let us make a covenant with thee” (Genesis 26:28). Twice a Philistine commander read the blessing of God on a wandering herdsman and came to make terms.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Phichol; the name belongs to the chief captain of Abimelech, king of Gerar, in the days of Abraham and of Isaac.

BEERSHEBA, n. The well of the oath, or well of seven; a place in the south of Canaan.
SOJOURNER, n. A temporary resident; a stranger or traveller who dwells in a place for a time.

corruption_summary: The witness of a believer's life is treated as a technique to be managed, when Scripture shows outsiders drawing the conclusion themselves from a blessing they could not account for.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the character of witness in the patriarchal narratives. Abraham did not preach to Abimelech and Phichol; they came to him, and the first thing out of their mouths was God is with thee in all that thou doest. The same thing happened to Isaac, from the same office, with the same words: we saw certainly that the LORD was with thee. Neither patriarch had engineered the impression, and both had in fact behaved badly toward these very men, each having passed off his wife as his sister in Gerar.

That last detail keeps the lesson from becoming a flattering one about exemplary living. The witness Phichol read was not the patriarchs' conduct but God's evident hand on them — flocks, wells, increase, protection — given to men whose failures the same chapters record without concealment. Scripture does command a blameless walk and says plainly that outsiders will glorify God by our good works. It also insists that the credit belongs where Phichol put it. A Philistine general looking at Abraham said God, not Abraham, and that is the correct reading of every such life.

pos: n. (priest of On, and father of Joseph's wife Asenath)
etymology: Egyptian, meaning he whom Ra has given — a name built on the sun-god of Heliopolis, the city Scripture calls On. He was priest of that cult, and his daughter became the mother of two tribes of Israel.
biblical_def: Pharaoh's elevation of Joseph came with an Egyptian name and an Egyptian marriage: “And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphnathpaaneah; and he gave him to wife Asenath the daughter of Potipherah priest of On. And Joseph went out over all the land of Egypt” (Genesis 41:45). The marriage is recorded again at the birth of the sons: “And unto Joseph were born two sons before the years of famine came, which Asenath the daughter of Potipherah priest of On bare unto him” (Genesis 41:50). And a third time when Jacob's house is numbered going down into Egypt: “And unto Joseph in the land of Egypt were born Manasseh and Ephraim, which Asenath the daughter of Potipherah priest of On bare unto him” (Genesis 46:20). Scripture gives the names Joseph chose for those boys, and they are a testimony rather than an assimilation: “And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh: For God, said he, hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house” (Genesis 41:51). The grandsons of a sun-priest were named in Hebrew, for the God of Jacob, and they became two tribes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) identifies On as Heliopolis, the city of the sun in Egypt; Potipherah was its priest and the father-in-law of Joseph.

PRIEST, n. A man who officiates in sacred offices; among pagans, one who conducts the worship of an idol.
ASSIMILATE, v.t. To bring to a likeness; to cause to resemble; to convert into a like substance.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures.

corruption_summary: The marriage is used to argue that Scripture is indifferent to religious intermarriage, or else it is explained away; the text simply records it and shows what Joseph did afterward.
corruption_paragraphs: Joseph's marriage to the daughter of a pagan priest is sometimes produced as evidence that the Bible's later prohibitions on intermarriage are inconsistent or merely ethnic. The comparison does not hold. Those prohibitions, given at Sinai and enforced by Ezra, concern the peoples of Canaan and the covenant community in the land, and their stated reason is religious: they will turn away thy son from following me. Joseph was a captive in Egypt, given a wife by the crown as part of an investiture he did not negotiate, before Sinai and before Israel was a nation. Genesis reports the arrangement without approving or condemning it.

The name itself faces no postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what Joseph did with the position. He received an Egyptian name, an Egyptian wife, and a chariot, and then he named his sons in Hebrew for what God had done — Manasseh, because God had made him forget his toil; Ephraim, because God had caused him to be fruitful in the land of his affliction. At the end of his life he took an oath of his brethren concerning his bones, because he believed the promise about a land he had not seen since he was seventeen. A man can be given a foreign name and a priest's daughter and remain, in the only sense that matters, unassimilated.

pos: n. (the father of Jehoshaphat the recorder)
etymology: Hebrew Achilud, meaning a brother born or child's brother. He is named only as the father of the man who kept the royal records through two reigns.
biblical_def: The cabinet lists of David and Solomon are among the most matter-of-fact passages in Scripture, and this man's son appears in all of them holding the same post: “And Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the host; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder” (2 Samuel 8:16). Years later, after Absalom's rebellion and Sheba's, the same list is given again with the same name in the same office: “And Adoram was over the tribute: and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder” (2 Samuel 20:24). And when the kingdom passes to Solomon the post survives the succession: “Elihoreph and Ahiah, the sons of Shisha, scribes; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, the recorder” (1 Kings 4:3). The recorder was the officer who kept the chronicles of the reign — what was done, when, and by whom. Nothing in the narrative turns on him. Yet the books of Samuel, Kings and Chronicles exist because such men did their work, and Scripture itself appeals to their archives: “Now the acts of David the king, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of Samuel the seer, and in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the book of Gad the seer” (1 Chronicles 29:29).

corruption_summary: Revelation is imagined as bypassing ordinary human labour, when the historical books rest on records kept by named officers over decades.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how inspiration and ordinary means work together. Chronicles repeatedly points the reader to its sources — the book of Samuel the seer, the book of Nathan the prophet, the book of the kings of Israel and Judah — and Luke opens his Gospel by saying that many had taken in hand to set forth a declaration, and that he had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, and would write in order. Scripture is not embarrassed by research, archives, and recorders.

This is exactly the Reformed doctrine of inspiration: the Spirit so carried the writers along that what they produced is the word of God, without suppressing their vocabulary, their personalities, or their use of records that a man like Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud had spent a working life compiling. A mechanical theory of dictation cannot account for the sources the Bible openly cites; a theory of merely human composition cannot account for what the finished books claim for themselves. The office of recorder, held by one man across two reigns and a civil war, is the quiet human substructure under books that are nevertheless God-breathed.

pos: n. (captain of the host of Hadarezer, slain by David)
etymology: Hebrew Shobak, of uncertain meaning; the Chronicler spells it Shophach. He commanded the Syrian army brought from beyond the river to fight Israel, and he died in the battle.
biblical_def: Beaten once, the Syrians escalated: “And Hadarezer sent, and brought out the Syrians that were beyond the river: and they came to Helam; and Shobach the captain of the host of Hadarezer went before them” (2 Samuel 10:16). The result is recorded without suspense: “And the Syrians fled before Israel; and David slew the men of seven hundred chariots of the Syrians, and forty thousand horsemen, and smote Shobach the captain of their host, who died there” (2 Samuel 10:18). The consequence was political: “And when all the kings that were servants to Hadarezer saw that they were smitten before Israel, they made peace with Israel, and served them. So the Syrians feared to help the children of Ammon any more” (2 Samuel 10:19). The war had begun over an insult — Hanun had shaved David's ambassadors and cut off their garments — and it ended with the Syrian confederacy dismantled. The next verse of the narrative is the one that matters most, because it opens the chapter of David's great fall: “And it came to pass, after the year was expired, at the time when kings go forth to battle, that David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel; and they destroyed the children of Ammon, and besieged Rabbah. But David tarried still at Jerusalem” (2 Samuel 11:1).

corruption_summary: Military success is read as the measure of a king's standing with God, when the narrative sets David's greatest victory immediately before his greatest sin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the arrangement of the narrative. Chapter 10 ends with the Syrian confederacy broken, Shobach dead, and every vassal king suing for peace — the high-water mark of David's reign. Chapter 11 begins with the words at the time when kings go forth to battle, and records that David sent Joab and tarried still at Jerusalem. The historian does not comment. He simply puts the two paragraphs side by side, and the reader who has followed the victory feels the sentence land.

The lesson is one Scripture teaches repeatedly and the church forgets as often: danger follows success more reliably than it follows failure. Hezekiah's pride came after the Assyrian was turned back; Uzziah was marvellously helped till he was strong, and when he was strong his heart was lifted up to his destruction. Paul's warning is the plainest form of it — let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall. Shobach fell at Helam and David fell in Jerusalem, and the second fall did more damage to Israel than the first army ever could.

pos: n. (an Assyrian and Babylonian court title: chief of the eunuchs)
etymology: Not a personal name but an office — Hebrew Rab saris, chief of the eunuchs or chief officer. It is borne by an Assyrian envoy sent against Hezekiah and by Babylonian princes at the fall of Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Three Assyrian officers by their titles come up against Jerusalem: “And the king of Assyria sent Tartan and Rabsaris and Rabshakeh from Lachish to king Hezekiah with a great host against Jerusalem. And they went up and came to Jerusalem” (2 Kings 18:17). A century and a half later the same title appears among the men who sat in the middle gate when the city fell: “And all the princes of the king of Babylon came in, and sat in the middle gate, even Nergalsharezer, Samgarnebo, Sarsechim, Rabsaris, Nergalsharezer, Rabmag, with all the residue of the princes of the king of Babylon” (Jeremiah 39:3). The same officers then execute an order concerning one prisoner: “So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard sent, and Nebushasban, Rabsaris, and Nergalsharezer, Rabmag, and all the king of Babylon's princes” (Jeremiah 39:13) — the prisoner being Jeremiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had specifically commanded be treated well. Hezekiah's answer to the first embassy is the pattern for both occasions: “And Hezekiah received the letter of the hand of the messengers, and read it: and Hezekiah went up into the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD” (2 Kings 19:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) treats Rab as a Chaldee title of office signifying chief or master; Rab-saris is the chief of the eunuchs or great officers.

corruption_summary: Titles are read as personal names and the passages become confused, while the real point — that great empires sent their highest officers and God answered a king who spread a letter before Him — is missed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle worth recovering is what the titles are doing in the narrative. Tartan, Rabsaris and Rabshakeh are offices, not men: commander-in-chief, chief officer, chief cupbearer. Assyria sent its three highest functionaries with a great host to demand a city's surrender, and the detail is there to establish scale. Against that, Hezekiah had a letter, a temple, and a prophet. The chapter is built so the reader feels the mismatch before the angel of the LORD goes out in the night.

The Babylonian occurrence carries the other half of the lesson. When Jerusalem finally fell, these same great officers sat in the middle gate as conquerors — and their first recorded act concerning an individual was to fetch Jeremiah out of the court of the prison and treat him kindly, because the king of Babylon had commanded it. The empire that God used to judge Judah was also the instrument by which He preserved the prophet who had announced the judgment. Hezekiah's response remains the model for both circumstances: he took the letter and spread it before the LORD, which is neither denial nor despair but prayer with the facts in hand.

pos: n. (an ancestor of Samuel, and the district named after him)
etymology: Hebrew Tsuph, meaning honeycomb. The name belongs to a Kohathite forefather of Samuel and to the territory in Ephraim that carried his name, where Saul was searching for lost asses when he met the prophet.
biblical_def: The first book of Samuel opens with a genealogy that reaches back to him: “Now there was a certain man of Ramathaimzophim, of mount Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephrathite” (1 Samuel 1:1). The Chronicler places the same man in the Levitical line, which explains how a family in Ephraim's hill country came to serve at the sanctuary: “The son of Zuph, the son of Elkanah, the son of Mahath, the son of Amasai” (1 Chronicles 6:35). The district took his name, and it is where the kingdom of Israel effectively began: “And when they were come to the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant that was with him, Come, and let us return; lest my father leave caring for the asses, and take thought for us” (1 Samuel 9:5). Saul was about to give up and go home. His servant suggested asking the man of God in the city, and the meeting that followed made him king. The narrator has already told the reader what was happening: “Now the LORD had told Samuel in his ear a day before Saul came, saying” (1 Samuel 9:15).

corruption_summary: Guidance is sought in impressions and signs, while Scripture shows an ordinary errand governed invisibly by a God who had already spoken to His prophet a day before.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how 1 Samuel 9 teaches providence. Saul is not on a spiritual quest; he is looking for his father's donkeys, and by the time he reaches the land of Zuph he is ready to abandon the search because his father will be worrying. Every step is ordinary: lost animals, a long walk, a discouraged young man, a servant with a practical suggestion and a quarter shekel of silver. And the narrator interrupts to say that the LORD had told Samuel in his ear a day before Saul came.

That sentence is the doctrine. Nothing in the errand announced itself as guidance; there was no impression, no sign, no inner voice, and Saul had no idea he was walking toward a throne. The Reformed understanding of God's leading rests here rather than on the modern search for personal revelations: God governs the whole chain of ordinary causes, and the believer's duty is obedience in the errand actually in front of him, whether that is a lost animal or a hard week. The wisdom to be sought is in the word already written; the arrangement of events belongs to the One who spoke to Samuel the day before.

pos: n. (a son of David born in Jerusalem; also one of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Eliphelet, meaning God is deliverance or God of escape. Several men carry it, including two of David's sons and a warrior in the roll of the thirty.
biblical_def: One bearer stands in the roll of David's mighty men: “Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite” (2 Samuel 23:34). The verse is worth reading twice, because the next name in it is Eliam the son of Ahithophel — and Eliam was Bathsheba's father, which makes Ahithophel her grandfather and goes some way to explaining why David's most gifted counsellor later joined Absalom's revolt. The other bearers are David's own sons, listed among those born to him in Jerusalem: “Ibhar also, and Elishama, and Eliphelet” (1 Chronicles 3:6), and again at the end of the same list: “And Elishama, and Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine” (1 Chronicles 3:8). The names David gave these sons are confessions — Eliphelet, God is deliverance; Eliada, God knows; Elishama, God has heard. A man who had spent years hunted in caves named his children after what God had proved to be.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Eliphelet; the Hebrew signifies God is deliverance, and the name belongs to sons of David and to one of his mighty men.
webster_full: ELIPHELET, n. A son of David born in Jerusalem; in Hebrew, God is deliverance.
DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression or any restraint; rescue from danger.
MIGHTY, a. Very strong; valiant; bold; having great power or physical strength.
COUNSELLOR, n. Any person who gives advice; particularly, one appointed to advise a king or state.
CONFESSION, n. Acknowledgment; the acknowledging of a fault or of the truth; a profession of faith.

corruption_summary: Naming is treated as a matter of taste, when in Scripture a name is a claim about God or about a circumstance, and the genealogies are full of such claims.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Hebrew names carry statements. David's Jerusalem-born sons are a small creed read in order: Elishama, God has heard; Eliada, God knows; Eliphelet, God is deliverance. The man who wrote this poor man cried, and the LORD heard him gave his children names that said the same thing every time they were called in to supper. Nathan and Solomon are on the same list, and so is Nathan's line, through which Luke traces the genealogy of Christ.

The mighty-men list carries a different kind of weight. Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite stands next to Eliphelet in 2 Samuel 23, and 2 Samuel 11:3 identifies Bathsheba as the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite — who is himself in the same roll of thirty, a few verses later. The three men most wronged in the Bathsheba affair were all in David's own list of decorated soldiers. Scripture supplies the connection without comment, as it usually does, and leaves the reader to feel what the roll of honour cost.

pos: n. (a son of David; also the father of a Syrian adversary and a Benjamite captain)
etymology: Hebrew Elyada, meaning God knows or God has known. The Chronicler preserves a variant, Beeliada, and notes the equivalence in the margin — a name changed to purge the syllable Baal from it.
biblical_def: He appears in the list of sons born to David at Jerusalem: “And Elishama, and Eliada, and Eliphalet” (2 Samuel 5:16). The Chronicler gives the same three: “And Elishama, and Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine” (1 Chronicles 3:8). But in another place the Chronicler records the older form of the name: “And Elishama, and Beeliada, and Eliphalet” (1 Chronicles 14:7) — Beeliada, meaning Baal knows. The same substitution appears elsewhere in Scripture: Ishbosheth was originally Eshbaal, and Mephibosheth was Meribbaal. As Israel came to understand what the Baal cult was, names built on that syllable were revised. Hosea records the LORD Himself announcing the change: “And it shall be at that day, saith the LORD, that thou shalt call me Ishi; and shalt call me no more Baali” (Hosea 2:16). The Hebrew baal simply means lord or husband, and was once used innocently; when it had been thoroughly claimed by an idol, God would not be addressed by it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Eliada; the Hebrew signifies God knows, and the name belongs to a son of David and to others.
webster_full: ELIADA, n. A son of David born in Jerusalem; in Hebrew, God knows.
BAAL, n. The chief male deity of the Phoenicians and Canaanites; in Hebrew, a lord, master, husband or possessor.
ISHI, n. In Hebrew, my husband; the title by which the LORD would be called instead of Baali.
EUPHEMISM, n. A figure of speech in which a harsh or offensive word is replaced by a milder one.
SYNCRETISM, n. The attempted union of principles or parties irreconcilably at variance.

corruption_summary: Borrowed religious vocabulary is defended as harmless on the ground that words are neutral, when Scripture shows God retiring a term that a rival worship had captured.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that words can be taken captive. Baal began as an ordinary Hebrew word for lord or husband, and Israelites used it in their children's names without any thought of the Canaanite storm-god. By Hosea's day the syllable had been so thoroughly annexed by an idol that the LORD announced He would no longer be addressed by it: thou shalt call me Ishi, and shalt call me no more Baali. The name Beeliada became Eliada, and Eshbaal became Ishbosheth, for the same reason.

The application is not that Christians should police vocabulary anxiously, but that they should notice when a word has changed owners. Much of the difficulty in modern theological argument is that terms both parties use — love, justice, inclusion, identity, even grace — have been redefined by a rival framework while keeping their old warmth. Hosea's remedy was not a campaign against a syllable but a change of address that made the object of worship unmistakable. Where a term can no longer be used without importing an alien meaning, the faithful course is to say plainly what is meant, as God did.

pos: n. (a chief of Benjamin; also one of David's mighty men and a temple porter)
etymology: Hebrew Yediael, meaning known of God. The chief bearer heads a Benjamite house numbered at more than seventeen thousand fighting men.
biblical_def: He stands among the sons of Benjamin: “The sons of Benjamin; Bela, and Becher, and Jediael, three” (1 Chronicles 7:6). His line is then traced: “The sons also of Jediael; Bilhan: and the sons of Bilhan; Jeush, and Benjamin, and Ehud, and Chenaanah, and Zethan, and Tharshish, and Ahishahar” (1 Chronicles 7:10). And the house is counted: “All these the sons of Jediael, by the heads of their fathers, mighty men of valour, were seventeen thousand and two hundred soldiers, fit to go out for war and battle” (1 Chronicles 7:11). The name means known of God, and Scripture applies that idea with precision: God's knowing is not mere awareness but acknowledgment and love. Paul states both halves in one sentence: “Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity” (2 Timothy 2:19). Seventeen thousand two hundred men of one Benjamite house are counted in a register; the seal Paul names counts a different muster, and misses none of it.

corruption_summary: Divine knowing is flattened into bare omniscience, so that a name meaning known of God loses the covenant sense Scripture gives the word.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the biblical force of the verb know when God is its subject. He knows all things as a matter of omniscience, including the number of hairs and the fall of a sparrow; that is not what Amos means when he says of Israel, You only have I known of all the families of the earth, nor what Paul means by the Lord knoweth them that are his, nor what Christ means in the terrible sentence, I never knew you. In those places knowing is acknowledgment, choice and love.

That distinction is the difference between a doctrine of election that comforts and one that frightens. If God's knowing His own were only foreknowledge of what they would do, assurance would rest at last on the believer's performance. Paul grounds it elsewhere: the foundation of God standeth sure, and its seal is that the Lord knows His own — with the second half of the seal following immediately, that everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity. The name Jediael, known of God, states in Hebrew what the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling states in Latin, and a man numbered in that register is not lost.

pos: n. (a descendant of Zerubbabel; also a Benjamite, a Levite, and a steward of Ahaz)
etymology: Hebrew Azriqam, meaning my help has arisen or help against the enemy. Four men bear it, and the last of them was killed in the same hour as a king's son.
biblical_def: The name runs down the royal line after the exile: “And the sons of Neariah; Elioenai, and Hezekiah, and Azrikam, three” (1 Chronicles 3:23) — that is, in the genealogy of Zerubbabel, the line by which the promise to David was carried through the captivity. A second bearer belongs to Saul's house in Benjamin: “And Azel had six sons, whose names are these, Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel” (1 Chronicles 8:38). A third is a Levite of the sons of Merari: “And of the Levites; Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari” (1 Chronicles 9:14). And a fourth held high office in Judah in its worst days and died when Israel invaded under Pekah: “And Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, slew Maaseiah the king's son, and Azrikam the governor of the house, and Elkanah that was next to the king” (2 Chronicles 28:7). The name means my help has arisen, and the man who bore it was cut down in the reign of Ahaz.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Azrikam; the Hebrew signifies my help has arisen, and four men of the name appear in the genealogies.

corruption_summary: The Davidic line is assumed to have ended at the exile, when Chronicles keeps tracing it generation by generation through the captivity to the men who came home.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the continuity of the promise. God had sworn to David that his seed would endure for ever and his throne as the days of heaven; then Jerusalem fell, the temple burned, the last king was blinded and carried to Babylon, and by every visible measure the covenant had failed. 1 Chronicles 3 keeps counting anyway — Jeconiah, Salathiel, Zerubbabel, Hananiah, Neariah, and the three sons of Neariah, of whom Azrikam is one. A genealogist went on writing names through the worst seventy years the nation ever had.

That is why the New Testament opens with a genealogy. Matthew runs the same line through the carrying away into Babylon and out the other side to Joseph the husband of Mary, and the whole point of the fourteen-and-fourteen-and-fourteen arrangement is that the promise survived the exile. A register kept during a catastrophe is an act of faith, and Chronicles is full of them. The man named my help has arisen who was killed under Ahaz did not see the help; the line he belonged to reached Bethlehem.
